analysis.one_liner: Doubles required overtime pay for workers from time-and-a-half to double time.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in June 2026 with 30 cosponsors (all Democrats), was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has seen no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes the Fair Labor Standards Act so that when an employee works more than 40 hours in a week, the employer must pay twice their regular hourly rate instead of the current 1.5 times. It would apply across the law's overtime rules, including special categories like certain seamen and retail commission employees, and would take effect 180 days after being signed into law.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly and salaried non-exempt workers who put in overtime hours would see their overtime pay jump from 1.5 times to 2 times their regular rate — for example, a worker earning $20 an hour would get $40 instead of $30 for each overtime hour. The raise would apply to every hour covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime rules, including the specific categories the bill amends such as certain seamen, motor carrier employees, and retail service commission employees [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who put in overtime hours

how_it_helps.text: Rewrites the Fair Labor Standards Act's overtime formula from 'one and one-half' times the regular rate to 'two' times, so every covered overtime hour pays double [S2].

Applies the doubled rate throughout the overtime law, including section 13 provisions covering specific groups such as certain seamen and retail commission employees, closing the loopholes where the old 1.5x rate was written in separately [S2].
Gives employers 180 days after enactment to adjust, so the increase would not hit paychecks immediately [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — businesses in retail, restaurants, hospitals, warehouses, and any operation that schedules more than 40 hours a week — would pay roughly 33% more for each overtime hour (from 1.5x to 2x the regular rate). Those costs would land on business margins, and some portion could be passed to customers through higher prices or absorbed by cutting scheduled overtime hours [S2].

drawbacks.text: Doubling the overtime rate makes each overtime hour 33% more expensive than the current 1.5x rate, giving employers a stronger incentive to cap hours at 40, spread work across more part-time staff, or automate — which could leave some workers with fewer total hours even as their overtime rate rises [S2].
The 180-day effective date gives businesses little lead time to re-plan staffing and budgets, a burden that falls hardest on small businesses with thin margins and unpredictable demand [S2].
Salaried non-exempt and piece-rate workers could see more complicated pay calculations, since the 'regular rate' the doubling is based on varies week to week [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and direct: millions of overtime hours worked each week would pay noticeably more. The cost falls on employers, and the honest caveat is that some of it does not stay there — businesses can respond by trimming overtime hours, adding part-time staff, or raising prices, which shifts part of the burden back to the very workers the bill targets and to consumers. The bill is a straight wage floor increase with no phase-in by business size, so its design amplifies those side effects for small employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Double the Wage for Overtime Act of 2026 on June 9, 2026, joined by 17 original cosponsors including Reps. Jayapal, Horsford, and Norton [S2].
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and Workforce the same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action since [S4].
All 30 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the committee it sits in is where such referrals typically end without majority support [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who rely on overtime labor are better off so far — the requirement to pay 1.5 times instead of double time remains the law because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who rely on overtime labor

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, making this a strictly one-party effort so far.

industries.industry: Overtime-heavy employers (retail, restaurants, hospitals, warehouses, manufacturing)
industries.note: Each overtime hour these businesses schedule would cost about 33% more (2x instead of 1.5x the regular rate), cutting directly into labor-cost-dependent margins. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the wage increase workers would get from it, though some cost would likely reach consumers through prices [S2].

Agencies that profit from placing long-hours workers would face higher overtime premiums on the hours they staff, but could also gain business from employers shifting work around the 40-hour threshold. The net effect depends on how each firm prices labor [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action weeks after referral, and a chamber agenda controlled by the other party, the realistic path is that the bill stays in the Education and Workforce Committee until the Congress ends — the same fate that met similar overtime-doubling bills in earlier Congresses. A discharge petition to force a floor vote would require 218 signatures and has virtually no chance without some Republican support.
